content.title: About
content.content: Chicken is a popular source of lean protein obtained from poultry meat. This product uses only skinless meat, which reduces fat and calorie content. Chicken can be prepared by boiling, baking, frying, stewing, or steaming.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken is the most consumed type of meat worldwide.
Chicken meat is rich in essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.
Skinless chicken contains roughly half the fat of meat with skin.
Chicken eggs and meat are staples in traditional dishes across many cultures.
Chicken can be raised in industrial or farm settings, affecting its nutritional profile.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken provides a complete source of protein essential for maintaining muscle mass and metabolism.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Removing the skin dramatically lowers saturated fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken supplies niacin (B3) and pyridoxine (B6), which support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It contains phosphorus, selenium, and zinc, important for bones, immunity, and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low calorie density
items.content: 100 g of skinless chicken breast provides about 110 kcal, helpful for weight management.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter, so it must be cooked thoroughly to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Excess sodium
items.content: Marinating or using pre‑made sauces can increase the sodium content.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Skinless chicken breast can be diced, sliced, or cooked whole. It can be boiled in broth, baked with herbs, pan‑fried with minimal oil, or steamed. Cooked chicken is used in salads, soups, stews, sandwiches, and pasta dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh chicken in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 9 months. Thaw in the refrigerator, not at room temperature.

content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate pancakes are thin fried cakes made from a batter of flour, milk and eggs, with melted dark chocolate or a chocolate filling added. The dish is popular in fast‑food outlets and restaurants as a quick sweet breakfast or dessert.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional pancakes originated in ancient Russia, while chocolate versions became widespread in the 20th century.
In Japan a similar dish called okonomiyaki is sometimes served with chocolate sauce, but in Russia chocolate pancakes are usually topped with butter and berries.
The Guinness World Record for the largest serving of chocolate pancakes weighs over 200 kg.
Chocolate pancakes are often served with ice cream, creating a hot‑cold contrast.
Vegetarians can make them without eggs, using substitutes such as flaxseed meal.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates from flour and sugar quickly provide glucose, useful before physical activity.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs and milk in the batter supply high‑quality protein needed for muscle repair.

items.title: Antioxidants from chocolate
items.content: Dark chocolate is rich in flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Milk adds calcium for bone health, and vitamin D improves its absorption.

items.title: Fiber when served with fruit
items.content: Adding berries or banana increases dietary fiber, supporting digestion.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Chocolate pancakes can contain a lot of sugar, which is unsuitable for people with diabetes.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Standard flour contains gluten; those with celiac disease should use gluten‑free alternatives.

items.title: Lactose
items.content: Milk in the batter may cause issues for individuals with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Chocolate pancakes are calorie‑dense; portion control is recommended to avoid overeating.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pancakes hot, drizzled with melted chocolate, dusted with powdered sugar, and garnished with berries, fruit slices or ice cream. They can be eaten with a fork and knife or rolled up like a wrap.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked pancakes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat on a skillet or in the microwave before serving to restore softness.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato sticks are crunchy snack sticks made from thinly sliced potatoes that are deep‑fried and coated with a flavored seasoning. They have a light, slightly salty taste with the characteristic aroma of the chosen spice blend.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Similar snacks first appeared in the United States in the early 20th century as “potato sticks”.
Seasonings can range from classic (sour cream & onion, barbecue) to exotic (chili‑lime, cheddar cheese).
Thin slicing gives a crisper texture compared with regular potato chips.
To achieve an even flavor, sticks are often tossed in a dry spice mix after frying.
In some countries they are also called “potato rods” or “potato straws”.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Potato sticks provide carbohydrates that quickly supply the body with energy.

items.title: Vitamin C content
items.content: When processed properly, some vitamin C is retained, supporting the immune system.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, important for fluid balance and muscle function.

items.title: Low sugar
items.content: Unlike many sweet snacks, potato sticks usually contain little simple sugar.

items.title: Convenient snack
items.content: Their crunchy texture and handy size make them a practical quick‑bite option.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Most of the calories come from fats absorbed during frying, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Salt
items.content: The salty flavor is achieved with added salt, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to potatoes.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: If partially hydrogenated oils are used, trans fats may be present.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Potato sticks are easy to enjoy as a standalone snack, added to salads, soups, or used as a crunchy base for dips. Serve them with various sauces such as sour cream, cheese dip, or guacamole.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For longer shelf life, store in the refrigerator to slow fat oxidation. Discard if the sticks become soft, lose aroma, or develop an off‑odor.

content.title: About
content.content: The Mexican roll “bolillo” is a soft wheat roll traditionally used in Mexico for sandwiches and burritos. The dough is made from wheat flour, water, yeast, salt, and a small amount of sugar, then shaped into small round rolls and baked until golden. Inside they stay soft, slightly airy, and mildly sweet.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bolillo comes from the Spanish word “bolillo,” meaning a small roll.
These rolls are a staple of Mexican street food, especially in “torta” meat sandwiches.
They are often served warm so the crust stays crisp while the crumb remains soft.
In some Mexican regions butter is added to the dough for a richer flavor.
A sweet version exists, flavored with cinnamon and sugar.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Bolillo provides quickly digestible carbs that supply energy.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The traditional recipe contains little added fat, making it a light snack.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour supplies B1, B3, and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: The roll contains a modest amount of fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Pairs well with protein
items.content: Bolillo is often used as a base for meat, fish, or bean dishes, helping to balance meals.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Bolillo contains wheat, so it is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Because of fast‑acting carbs, it can raise blood sugar quickly, which diabetics should monitor.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salt is commonly added to the dough; excess intake should be limited.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the bolillo horizontally and fill it with meat, chicken, avocado, vegetables, cheese, or beans. It also works as a base for sandwiches, served with sauces, salsa, or guacamole. For extra crunch, lightly toast the roll before filling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep bolillo in a paper bag or container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, place it in an airtight bag and refrigerate for up to 5 days or freeze for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Pickled seaweed is made from dried and then re‑hydrated marine algae, usually from the Porphyra (nori) or Laminaria families. It has a distinctive salty‑sour flavor, a crisp texture, and a vivid green color. The product is common in Asian cuisines, used in salads, sushi rolls, and as a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Seaweed is one of the richest natural sources of iodine, essential for thyroid function.
In Japan, nori is a staple food and appears in more than 70 % of all sushi rolls.
There are over 10,000 species of marine algae, but only a small fraction are edible.
Pickling helps preserve nutrients and extends shelf life to several months.
In traditional Korean cuisine, fermented seaweed (miyeok) is served as a side dish.

items.title: Rich in iodine
items.content: Iodine supports the production of thyroid hormones that regulate metabolism.

items.title: High in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Seaweed contains polyphenols and carotenoids that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It provides calcium, iron, magnesium, and potassium, which are vital for various bodily functions.

items.title: Excess iodine
items.content: Too much iodine can disrupt thyroid function, especially in susceptible individuals.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Pickled seaweed is salty; people with hypertension should limit their intake.

items.title: Seaweed allergy
items.content: Rare, but some individuals may experience allergic reactions.

items.title: Contaminants
items.content: Algae can accumulate heavy metals from the ocean; choose products from reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pickled seaweed can be eaten straight as a snack, added to salads, sushi rolls, soups, or used as a garnish. It is often rinsed briefly to reduce excess brine before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed container in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C. Shelf life is typically 3–6 months. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Strawberry milk, whole, is a beverage made from whole cow's milk blended with natural strawberry puree and a touch of sugar. It has a smooth creamy base with a bright berry flavor and retains all the nutrients of whole milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Strawberry milk is often served in schools and day‑care centers as a tasty way to increase milk consumption.
The strawberries used provide vitamin C and antioxidants that boost immunity.
In some countries it is a traditional summer refresher.
Only natural puree is used to achieve the vivid pink color, without artificial dyes.
Whole milk typically contains about 3.5 % fat.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Strawberry milk retains the full calcium content of whole milk, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Milk supplies riboflavin (B2) and cobalamin (B12), supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Vitamin C from strawberries
items.content: The strawberry puree adds vitamin C, enhancing the drink's antioxidant capacity.

items.title: Protein
items.content: A serving provides about 8 g of high‑quality protein for growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Probiotics (when cultured)
items.content: If the milk is pasteurized with live cultures, it can help maintain a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People who are lactose intolerant should choose lactose‑free versions or limit intake.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein or whey can cause reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Added sugar
items.content: The added sugar increases calorie content; those monitoring blood sugar should account for it.

items.title: Strawberry acidity
items.content: Children with sensitive stomachs may experience mild discomfort from the fruit's acidity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink it chilled as a refreshing beverage, blend it into smoothies, add to cereals, desserts, or use as a base for fruit cocktails.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 1‑4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3‑5 days. Do not freeze, as it may alter texture.
